subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Control of blood glucose and diabetes

questions.q: What is homeostasis?
options: The regulation of internal conditions to maintain a stable environment for cell function
The movement of water into cells
questions.explain: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions (e.g. temperature, blood glucose, water levels) to maintain optimum conditions for enzyme action and cell function, in response to internal and external change.

questions.q: A control system in homeostasis needs receptors, a coordination centre and:
options: Effectors that bring about a response
questions.explain: Automatic control systems have receptors (detect stimuli), coordination centres (brain, spinal cord, pancreas) and effectors (muscles or glands) that bring about responses to restore optimum levels.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes a nervous response?
options: stimulus -> receptor -> sensory neurone -> CNS -> motor neurone -> effector -> response
questions.explain: The pathway is: stimulus detected by a receptor, sensory neurone carries impulses to the CNS, then a motor neurone carries impulses to an effector (muscle or gland) which produces a response.

questions.q: What happens at a synapse between two neurones?
options: A chemical (neurotransmitter) diffuses across the gap and triggers an impulse in the next neurone
The electrical impulse jumps straight across the gap
questions.explain: At a synapse there is a tiny gap. A chemical (neurotransmitter) is released, diffuses across the gap, and binds to the next neurone to set off a new electrical impulse.

questions.q: Why are reflex actions important?
options: They are automatic and rapid, protecting the body from harm
questions.explain: Reflex actions are automatic and rapid and do not involve the conscious part of the brain, so they protect the body (e.g. pulling a hand off a hot object). They travel along a reflex arc.

questions.q: Which part of the eye changes shape to focus light on the retina (accommodation)?
questions.explain: The lens changes shape during accommodation: it becomes thicker/more curved to focus on near objects and thinner to focus on distant objects. The ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments control this.

questions.q: In bright light, the pupil reflex causes the pupil to:
options: Get larger to let in more light
Get smaller to protect the retina from damage
Close completely and stop all light
questions.explain: In bright light the circular muscles of the iris contract and the radial muscles relax, making the pupil smaller. This reduces the light entering the eye and protects the retina from damage.

questions.q: Which part of the brain monitors and controls body temperature?
options: The thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus
questions.explain: The thermoregulatory centre in the brain (hypothalamus) contains receptors sensitive to blood temperature, and it receives information from temperature receptors in the skin.

questions.q: When the body is too hot, which response helps to cool it down?
options: Sweating and vasodilation (more blood flow near the skin surface)
questions.explain: When too hot, sweat is produced (evaporation transfers energy away) and blood vessels near the skin dilate (vasodilation) so more heat is lost. Shivering and vasoconstriction happen when too cold.

questions.q: How do hormones travel to their target organs?
options: Through the air sacs of the lungs
questions.explain: The endocrine system uses glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, which carries them to target organs. Hormonal effects are generally slower but longer-lasting than nervous responses.

questions.q: Which gland is often called the 'master gland' because it secretes hormones that control other glands?
questions.explain: The pituitary gland in the brain is the 'master gland': it secretes several hormones in response to body conditions, and these act on other glands to release further hormones.

questions.lo: Control of blood glucose and diabetes
questions.q: When blood glucose concentration is too high, the pancreas releases which hormone?
questions.explain: When blood glucose is too high, the pancreas releases insulin, which causes glucose to move from the blood into cells; in the liver and muscles it is stored as glycogen. This lowers blood glucose.

questions.lo: Control of blood glucose and diabetes
questions.q: What is the main difference between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?
options: In Type 1 the pancreas produces little or no insulin; in Type 2 the body cells stop responding well to insulin
Type 1 is caused by eating too much sugar only
Type 2 always requires insulin injections from birth
questions.explain: In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas makes little or no insulin (usually treated with insulin injections). In Type 2 the body cells no longer respond properly to insulin; it is linked to obesity and often managed by diet and exercise.

questions.q: By which processes does the body lose water that it cannot control?
options: Through the lungs when breathing out and the skin in sweat
questions.explain: Water is lost in an uncontrolled way via the lungs (breathing out) and the skin (sweating, which also loses ions). Excess water, ions and urea are removed in a controlled way by the kidneys in urine.

questions.q: Where is excess amino acid converted to urea before excretion? (Higher tier)
questions.explain: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver to form ammonia, which is toxic and immediately converted to urea. Urea is transported by the blood to the kidneys, where it is filtered out and excreted in urine.

questions.q: Which hormone controls the amount of water reabsorbed by the kidneys? (Higher tier)
questions.explain: ADH (anti-diuretic hormone) is released by the pituitary gland and controls water reabsorption in the kidney tubules. More ADH means more water reabsorbed and more concentrated urine. This is negative feedback.

questions.q: During kidney dialysis, why is the dialysis fluid made with a normal blood-plasma concentration of glucose and useful ions?
options: To remove the red blood cells
So useful substances are not lost from the blood, while urea and excess ions diffuse out
So all the patient's glucose diffuses out into the fluid
To add urea to the blood
questions.explain: Dialysis fluid contains normal levels of glucose and ions so there is no concentration gradient for these useful substances to be lost. Urea (absent from the fluid) and excess ions diffuse out of the blood down their gradients.

questions.q: Which hormone causes an egg to mature in the ovary during the menstrual cycle? (Higher tier)
questions.explain: FSH, released by the pituitary gland, causes an egg to mature in the ovary and stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen. LH triggers ovulation, and oestrogen and progesterone maintain the uterus lining.

questions.q: How do hormonal contraceptives such as the pill prevent pregnancy?
options: By using oestrogen and/or progesterone to inhibit FSH so no eggs mature
questions.explain: The combined pill contains oestrogen and progesterone. High oestrogen inhibits FSH production so eggs do not mature; progesterone thickens the cervical mucus. Barrier methods (condoms) physically stop sperm.

questions.q: Which plant hormone controls phototropism and gravitropism by causing unequal growth? (Higher tier)
questions.explain: Auxin controls growth responses. It gathers on the shaded side of a shoot, causing that side to grow more so the shoot bends towards light (positive phototropism). Auxins are used commercially as weedkillers and rooting powders.
